theme_scores.justification: Sets a clear quantified goal (30,000 more apprenticeships, measured 2015-2020) and describes a process of re-evaluation at the end of the period and five interim success areas, but gives no detail on how results will be published or acted on.

Lays out a concrete, timetabled monitoring process—quarterly data collection coordinated by Cabinet Office, baseline established by end of FY2016/17, then yearly review, tied to the April 2017 legislative target—but never states whether or how results will be published.
Identifies outcome measures (career progression, retention, reduced contingent labour) but gives no timetable or explanation of how or when this tracking will be evaluated or reported.
States intent to monitor diversity of apprentice intakes from 1 April 2016 but offers no method, timetable, or evaluation/publication plan beyond the bare monitoring statement.
Proposes an employer survey to assess productivity and return on investment but provides no frequency, timetable, or indication of what will be done with the findings.

reasoning: The core themes together show the document has moved past vague ambition into a structured monitoring regime: quarterly data requests coordinated by the Cabinet Office, a baseline to be set by "the end of the financial year 2016/17," annual review thereafter, and governance oversight by Cabinet Office—tied to the April 2017 legislative target. This satisfies level 2's requirement for 'comprehensive success measures, or the process for developing them,' and gives real detail on monitoring/evaluation timing. However, none of the core themes—including the strongest, Data Collection and Monitoring—say what will happen to the results once collected: there is no mention of publication, external reporting, or how findings will feed into policy change beyond internal review ('internally reviewed', 'maintain clear governance'). The weaker core themes (Diversity, Long-Term Tracking, Productivity) rely on single-line intentions to monitor via surveys or data without timetables of their own, which prevents the overall package from being uniformly comprehensive. There is also no discussion of testing the policy before rollout, nor any justification for omitting testing, though this may be appropriate for a workforce programme. Given the solid monitoring architecture but the absence of any stated publication or results-use plan, the document clearly meets level 2 but falls short of level 3. To reach level 3, it would need to state clearly when and how monitoring/evaluation findings will be published or used to adjust the programme.
